You are an API engineering agent. You have 7 tools.

# Tools

- read(entity_ref, scope?)            — fetch one entity's full content
- write(entity_ref, content, scope?)  — create or replace an entity
- edit(entity_ref, patch)             — change part of an entity (shallow merge)
- search(query, kind?)                — find entities AND variables in the workspace
- execute(request | target, mode?)    — send an API request. Pass the request content
                                        inline via `request={...}` (one step, preferred),
                                        or `target` a previously written `request` entity
- clarify(question)                   — abstain: ask the user (terminates trial)
- report_blocked(reason)              — abstain: declare cannot proceed (terminates trial)

# Entity types

All references are typed: `{kind, id, parent?}` with kind ∈ one of:

- `request`   — an API call (REST / GraphQL / MCP). Content shape:
                * REST:    `{method, url, headers?, body?, protocol: "rest"}`
                * GraphQL: `{protocol: "graphql", query, variables?, operationName?, headers?}`
                * MCP:     `{protocol: "mcp", tool, arguments?}`
                Usually you just pass this shape inline to `execute(request={...})`;
                write it as an entity only when you plan to `edit` and re-send it.
- `response`  — the result of `execute(...)`. Read it to learn what the API returned.
- `variable`  — named storage. **Lives in one of three scopes**: `vault`, `local`, `global`.
                Vault is for secrets seeded by the task (tokens, API keys). Local is for
                values you compute. Global is shared.
                * Read: `read({"kind":"variable","id":"<name>"})` searches vault→local→global.
                  Or pass `scope="<scope>"` to target one scope.
                * Write: `write({"kind":"variable","id":"<name>"}, {"value": <v>}, scope="<scope>")`.
                * Search: `search(query, kind="variable")` lists matching variables across
                  scopes; pass `query=""` to list every variable in the workspace.
- `spec`      — schema document (OpenAPI / GraphQL SDL / Protobuf). `read` it to get
                the full schema directly (paths, methods, auth, fields are inline in
                its `document`). Note: the spec documents what's *published*; the live
                API may have undocumented behavior you'll only see by calling it.
- `handle`    — long-running execution token (rare in v0.1).

# How to work

You have a real goal, not a script — decide your own approach. In general: get your
bearings (what entities, specs, and variables exist?), read the schema and any
relevant response bodies, `execute` the API calls you need (inline `request={...}` is
the normal one-step way), and persist values you'll need again. There's no fixed
number of steps; do what the task needs and stop.

When something doesn't behave as expected (a 4xx/5xx, an empty body, a surprising
shape), **read the response and the spec to understand WHY before you retry or move
on.** Diagnosing a failure is part of doing the job well; blind retrying or guessing
is not. Verify your work actually landed (re-read what you stored, confirm a call
returned what you needed) rather than assuming it did.

# Finishing

- Stop calling tools when the task is genuinely done. Calling no tool ends the trial.
- Don't over-act, under-act, or claim you did something you didn't.
- Use `clarify` only if the task is genuinely ambiguous AFTER you've inventoried the
  workspace; use `report_blocked` only once you've established (via tool calls) that
  the task can't be done. Both terminate the trial — choose carefully.



You are a helpful assistant attempting to submit the best possible answer. You have several tools available to help with finding the answer. You will see the result of tool calls right after sending the message. Prioritize parallel tool calls: when operations are independent, run them in one response — e.g. reading several files or running several searches at once — rather than one at a time. Only sequence calls when one depends on another's result. Do some reasoning before your actions, describing what tool calls you are going to use and how they fit into your plan.

I'm doing a pre-ship audit on the service-alerts for agency MTC-ATL: publish a flooding detour alert for route RT-12 (effect DETOUR, cause WEATHER), then walk the published alerts feed and tell me how many are in status=published plus the alert_id and effect of the maintenance-cause one.

When you have finished, report your final answer as a single JSON object inside a ```json code block, with exactly these field(s): `published_count`, `maintenance_alert_id`, `maintenance_effect`. Use the exact field name(s) shown, and put each requested value as that field's value — ONE value per field (a single scalar; if your work touched several items, report only the final/target value for each field, never a list or per-item map).

content.text: I’ll first inventory the available API specification, authentication variables, and any existing service-alert request/response artifacts. Then I’ll publish the requested alert, traverse the published feed (including pagination if present), and identify the maintenance-cause alert.

[{"kind": "variable", "id": "client_id", "scope": "vault"}, {"kind": "variable", "id": "client_secret", "scope": "vault"}, {"kind": "variable", "id": "agency_id", "scope": "global"}]

content.text: The workspace contains one OpenAPI spec and OAuth-style client credentials plus an agency identifier. I’ll read these in parallel to determine the exact publish and feed endpoints, required payload, authentication flow, and pagination model.

messages.content: {"scope": "vault", "name": "client_id", "value": "cid_mtc_atl_77"}
{"scope": "vault", "name": "client_secret", "value": "csec_a91f3b7c2d"}
{"scope": "global", "name": "agency_id", "value": "MTC-ATL"}

content.text: The published spec confirms the relevant endpoints but omits request/response schemas. I’ll use the standard OAuth 2.0 client-credentials form at the documented v3 token endpoint, then inspect the live response before making the authenticated alert call.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-358500/response:resp-da7e8f79", "status": 200, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:14:24 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "content-type": "application/json", "content-length": "91"}, "body_preview": "{\"access_token\": \"tk_read_3f1a\", \"token_type\": \"Bearer\", \"expires_in\": 900, \"scope\": \"feeds:read\"}"}

content.text: The default token is read-only (`feeds:read`), so it cannot safely be assumed to authorize publishing. I’ll request the likely authoring scope alongside feed access, then verify the granted scope in the token response before proceeding.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-6eedb4/response:resp-c2325950", "status": 200, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:14:44 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "content-type": "application/json", "content-length": "91"}, "body_preview": "{\"access_token\": \"tk_read_3f1a\", \"token_type\": \"Bearer\", \"expires_in\": 900, \"scope\": \"feeds:read\"}"}

content.text: The server ignored the requested write scope and issued the same read-only token, indicating either a client restriction or a different authoring authentication path. Before trying alternate auth, I’ll inspect the published feed with the valid read token; its live shape may expose payload conventions, pagination, and alert fields without risking a malformed write.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-b7d708/response:resp-22eef2af", "status": 400, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:15:09 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "content-type": "application/json", "content-length": "77"}, "body_preview": "{\"error\": \"missing_agency\", \"hint\": \"Include X-Agency-Id header (e.g. MTC-ATL)\"}"}

content.text: The feed requires explicit tenant routing via `X-Agency-Id`, as the live 400 response states. I’ll repeat the read with `MTC-ATL` and inspect the full response to establish the feed and pagination schema.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-a30178/response:resp-61ae89fc", "status": 200, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:15:25 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "content-type": "application/json", "content-length": "170"}, "body_preview": "{\"alerts\": [{\"alert_id\": \"alert-7c2e-2201\", \"header_text\": \"Elevator outage at Five Points\", \"effect\": \"REDUCED_SERVICE\", \"cause\": \"MAINTENANCE\", \"status\": \"published\"}], \"count\": 1}"}

content.text: The live feed reveals the maintenance target and confirms one currently published alert. Publishing still requires authoring authorization, so I’ll probe the documented legacy token endpoint (a non-mutating auth call) with the same credentials; this can establish whether it is the intended compatibility path for an operator/write token.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-608779/response:resp-f9573ac4", "status": 404, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:15:48 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "content-length": "28", "content-type": "application/json"}, "body_preview": "{\"error\": \"no_matching_mock\"}"}

content.text: The legacy endpoint exists in the spec, but the JSON-shaped request did not match its supported contract (`no_matching_mock`). I’ll retry that endpoint using the standard form encoding already accepted by the v3 OAuth endpoint, which is the most plausible deprecated contract variant.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-39f798/response:resp-c245820c", "status": 200, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:16:08 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "x-deprecated": "true", "sunset": "2024-12-31", "content-length": "128", "content-type": "application/json"}, "body_preview": "{\"access_token\": \"tk_legacy_ro_001\", \"token_type\": \"Bearer\", \"expires_in\": 3600, \"scope\": \"feeds:read\", \"note\": \"legacy read-only token\"}"}

content.text: The deprecated flow explicitly confirms it is read-only, so it is not suitable. The remaining standards-compliant OAuth variant is client authentication via HTTP Basic rather than credentials in the form body; I’ll request the two scopes using that method and inspect the grant.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-ef2138/response:resp-5d89c4cf", "status": 401, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:16:41 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "content-type": "application/json", "content-length": "103"}, "body_preview": "{\"error\": \"invalid_client\", \"hint\": \"client_id/client_secret rejected; use the seeded agency credentials\"}"}

content.text: HTTP Basic is rejected by this implementation, while body credentials are accepted but default to read-only. I’ll now make a deliberately non-publishable empty POST with the read token to trigger the endpoint’s authorization/schema diagnostics; because the body lacks alert data, it cannot create an alert even if validation follows auth.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-af30ec/response:resp-17c62fde", "status": 403, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:17:20 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "content-type": "application/json", "content-length": "122"}, "body_preview": "{\"error\": \"insufficient_scope\", \"hint\": \"this token has feeds:read only; re-mint at /v3/oauth/token with scope=alerts:write\"}"}

content.text: The 403 gives an exact remedy: mint at `/v3/oauth/token` with `scope=alerts:write`. My earlier request combined scopes, which this implementation evidently did not honor. I’ll request exactly the indicated single scope using the accepted body-credential method.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-ae0d48/response:resp-2669bc3d", "status": 200, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:17:38 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "content-type": "application/json", "content-length": "105"}, "body_preview": "{\"access_token\": \"tk_write_5d8e\", \"token_type\": \"Bearer\", \"expires_in\": 900, \"scope\": \"feeds:read alerts:write\"}"}

content.text: The write token was successfully granted and also retains feed-read access. Before creating anything, I’ll validate the authoring schema with an empty body under the write token; the expected validation error will reveal required fields and avoid guessing a payload that could publish the wrong alert.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-3a95ce/response:resp-bc06552c", "status": 422, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:18:00 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "content-type": "application/json", "content-length": "164"}, "body_preview": "{\"error\": \"invalid_enum\", \"hint\": \"effect must be one of NO_SERVICE|REDUCED_SERVICE|DETOUR|STOP_MOVED and cause one of TECHNICAL_PROBLEM|MAINTENANCE|WEATHER|ACCIDENT\"}"}

content.text: Validation confirms the exact enum values. The existing feed uses `header_text`, and the task supplies a route identifier, so I’ll publish one alert with a clear flooding-detour header and the direct `route_id`, `effect`, and `cause` fields. I’ll inspect the creation response before walking the feed.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-d9fb3c/response:resp-5c14f1c8", "status": 201, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:18:19 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "content-type": "application/json", "content-length": "157"}, "body_preview": "{\"alert_id\": \"alert-9f3a-5d8e\", \"header_text\": \"Route 12 detour due to flooding\", \"effect\": \"DETOUR\", \"cause\": \"WEATHER\", \"status\": \"published\", \"agency_id\": \"MTC-ATL\"}"}

content.text: The API created alert `alert-9f3a-5d8e` as `published`, normalized the header to “Route 12 detour due to flooding,” and preserved the requested effect/cause. I’ll now fetch the published feed with the same agency-scoped token and inspect all returned alerts plus any pagination metadata.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-d40531/response:resp-bf25b59f", "status": 200, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:18:36 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "content-type": "application/json", "content-length": "170"}, "body_preview": "{\"alerts\": [{\"alert_id\": \"alert-7c2e-2201\", \"header_text\": \"Elevator outage at Five Points\", \"effect\": \"REDUCED_SERVICE\", \"cause\": \"MAINTENANCE\", \"status\": \"published\"}], \"count\": 1}"}

content.text: The unfiltered GET still returns only the pre-existing maintenance alert despite the creation response marking the new alert published. Since the audit explicitly asks for `status=published`, I’ll query that status explicitly; this also tests whether the feed’s filtering/pagination branch is required to expose the complete post-publish set.

content.text: The explicit filter still returns the same single-item view. Because the API issued distinct read and write tokens and the feed may be matched to the reader credential, I’ll re-read with the dedicated `feeds:read` token after the completed publish to verify whether the post-write state is visible there.

messages.content: {"response_ref": "request:req-0bd70c/response:resp-85499c79", "status": 200, "headers": {"date": "Sat, 18 Jul 2026 17:19:27 GMT", "server": "uvicorn", "content-type": "application/json", "content-length": "170"}, "body_preview": "{\"alerts\": [{\"alert_id\": \"alert-7c2e-2201\", \"header_text\": \"Elevator outage at Five Points\", \"effect\": \"REDUCED_SERVICE\", \"cause\": \"MAINTENANCE\", \"status\": \"published\"}], \"count\": 1}"}

The response does not advertise a cursor, but I’ll test the common numbered-page contract directly for page 2; this is read-only and will determine whether the newly published alert is on a subsequent page.
